<reason>Both sides were competent and the clash narrowed properly, but PRO's load-bearing claim — the buyer paid a one-time ownership price, the seller's obligation was discharged, and on death the seller keeps both money and goods — was never squarely neutralized. PRO's cleanest rebuttal disarmed CON's analogies (gyms, leases, subscriptions end because payments are ongoing), and CON's reply (hosting/servers as "ongoing infrastructure," lifetime gym membership) was asserted rather than developed into any continuing cost that justifies reversion. PRO also materially damaged CON's central economic claim: resale is voluntary, repeatable, immediate and therefore price-moving, whereas death is unschedulable and generational, so "one estate, one non-duplicating transfer" is not a resale market with extra steps. CON's fallback to the endless chain was clever, but its friction framing ("it's the friction, not the principle") was successfully turned by PRO in closing as a concession on principle plus a supplied substitute friction. CON's strongest weapon — PRO's conditional admission that if publishers flee to subscriptions "heirs lose nothing" — was pressed hard and honestly, and it does expose a contingency in the guarantee; but PRO answered it directly (CON's own account implies nothing was inherited anyway; rent/buy tiers already coexist) and reframed the weighing as certain present destruction of estates versus speculative repricing, which reads as the stronger comparison. CON's next-of-kin drafting objection stayed partly live, but PRO's "that asks for a better clause, not for estates to be destroyed" is adequate for a principle motion. CON also carried two clipped turns, losing the end of its opening cost argument and its "third category" answer, an execution cost. Both sides used proper A1:/A2: labelling and avoided fake sourcing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A2.1]-[A2.4]: showing CON's gym/lease/subscription analogies all rest on recurring payments that do not exist here, then severing the resale analogy on the ground that mortality is involuntary, unrepeatable and decades-distant, so "nobody prices a market off mortality." This gutted CON's economic collapse story, forcing CON to retreat to the softer generational-chain claim, which PRO then turned via CON's own "friction, not principle" concession.</best_rebuttal>
